idiom_name: AutoCloseable + try-with-resources; close() as the check-in for borrowed resources
implementation_notes: Java absorbs the release side into the language: try-with-resources guarantees close() on every exit path and suppresses close-time exceptions behind the body's, so the hand-back is the resource's own close method. Return the narrowest AutoCloseable interface the client must release and let the producer define what close means - a pooled JDBC connection's close returns the connection to the pool instead of closing the socket - so a lending API returns a type whose close hands back and keeps the pool's destroy path internal. The classic C++ structure has no direct analogue because references are not owned; interface typing plus try-with-resources is what carries the contract, and it remains justified to wrap a legacy non-AutoCloseable handle in the borrower's code rather than at the API.
pitfalls: close() on a pooled object usually means 'return', but the interface cannot enforce it: holding a raw driver Connection (or calling a pool's destroy method) breaks the invariant silently.
Explicitly closing twice is legal for AutoCloseable only when the implementation makes it so; naive pool proxies that return the same object twice corrupt the free list.
try-with-resources closes in reverse declaration order and a close failure is suppressed behind the body's exception, so a failed hand-back can disappear unless getSuppressed() is read.
Letting the resource escape the try block (stored in a field, returned, captured by a lambda) closes it while the escaped reference is still in use.
